title: Securtxn
tagline: SecurTxn is control layer that verifies identity before money moves
description:
THE PROBLEM

About $226 billion a year moves in B2B stablecoin payments, and none of it can
be recalled. When a payout goes to the wrong recipient, there is no chargeback
and no reversal. What exists instead is a recovery industry: Binance processes
roughly 4,000 deposit-retrieval requests a month, and Kraken charges $200 to
$500 per attempt. Recovering a misdirected payment is a support ticket. Not
sending one is a control.

Traditional banking solved this in 2020 with Confirmed Payee, which checks the
name on the account before a transfer goes out. Stablecoin rails have no
equivalent. A wallet address carries no identity, so nothing on the payment
path can answer the only question that matters: does this address actually
belong to the vendor on the invoice?

https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/2026/08/06/why-stablecoins-still-have-a-payment-recovery-problem/

SecurTxn is that missing control layer.

WHAT IT DOES

SecurTxn sits in front of a stablecoin payout and refuses to let it proceed
until three independent questions are answered:

1. Is the payee who they claim to be?
2. Is a live human approving this specific payment?
3. Is this address allowed to hold the asset at all?

Each is answered by a different system, and none of them can be satisfied by
the person trying to get paid.

HOW IT WORKS

Onboarding. A vendor connects a wallet and completes a real DigiLocker consent
flow, which returns their Aadhaar and PAN documents with a verifiable XML
signature. They then sign an EIP-712 wallet control proof and an identity
binding that ties the DigiLocker subject to that specific address. Only the
combination makes a wallet CONFIRMED. Identity documents are encrypted at rest
and reduced to HMAC digests for matching.

On-chain KYC (Hedera). The platform issues a verifiable credential for the
confirmed wallet and calls grantKyc on a tokenised bond deployed with the
Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (security 0.0.10444329, internal KYC
activated). This is the control that cannot be talked around: the token itself
rejects transfers to addresses that were never granted. An unverified wallet
does not fail our validation, it reverts on chain.

Consent before matching. When a payment is raised, the payee is notified and
must accept it with an EIP-712 signature before any identity check runs. This
ordering is deliberate. Running a match without consent would turn the product
into a lookup service that tells a stranger whether a given address belongs to
a given PAN.

The match (Chainlink CRE). The identity comparison runs inside a Confidential
Workflow on a Chainlink DON, in a TEE. The enclave never sees a name or a PAN.
It receives HMAC digests, compares them as opaque bytes, and returns one of
four verdicts: MATCHED, IDENTITY_MISMATCH, WALLET_NOT_ON_FILE or
VENDOR_NOT_FOUND. There is a single reason code for any identity failure,
because reporting which field mismatched would hand a prober a second bit of
information. The enclave has no crypto library and does no name scoring, so
there is nothing in it to leak.

Proof of personhood (World ID). The sender passes a World ID Selfie Check on
every payment, unconditionally. The payee is challenged only when the risk
engine asks for one: a first payment from this sender, an amount above their
tier ceiling, a recently rotated wallet, a stale check, or a recent identity
mismatch. Signals are role-qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>, so one human acting as both sides of a payment cannot
satisfy both checks with the same proof.

Settlement. The payout moves as an HTS token through an HTLC on Hedera testnet.
The payee claims it by revealing the preimage from their own key, which makes
the reveal itself the receipt. Nobody can produce it on their behalf, and an
unclaimed payment returns to the sender after the timelock.

Evidence. Every decision writes an evidence record. Records are batched into a
Merkle tree and anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10454706).
Each anchor reads itself back from a mirror node after writing, so an anchor is
verified against the public record rather than merely submitted. Any single
record can produce a standalone inclusion proof, and altering a record after
anchoring makes its proof stop matching.

Exception desk. A refusal is not a dead end. Blocked payments open a case with
the reason code, the evidence trail, and a path to resolution, because the
finance team still has an invoice to pay.

WHAT IS REAL

This is deployed and runs end to end at https://www.securtxn.com with no mocks
in the path. Two people have completed the full flow with their own DigiLocker
identities, their own World ID enrolments, a verdict from the deployed TEE
workflow, and a real token transfer on Hedera testnet.

One thing stated plainly: the asset moved in the demo is stUSDC, a test
stablecoin we issued on Hedera testnet, not Circle's USDC. The mechanics are
identical, an HTS fungible token moving between KYC gated accounts through the
escrow contract, but it should not be described as transferring USDC.


TECH STACK
==========

Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio bond with internal KYC, HTS token, HTLC
escrow contract, Hedera Consensus Service for evidence anchoring, mirror node
verification.

Chainlink CRE: Confidential Workflow with a TEE handler, deployed to a DON,
secrets held in the Vault DON, digest-only matching.

World ID: Selfie Check proof of personhood, role-qualified signals, nullifier
continuity enforced against enrolment.

Identity: DigiLocker via the Sandbox aggregator, Aadhaar and PAN with XML
signature verification.

Application: TypeScript, Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Next.js, viem, EIP-712
throughout.
how_its_made:
ARCHITECTURE

A pnpm monorepo. Fastify and Prisma over PostgreSQL (Supabase) for the API,
Next.js for the web app, viem for all chain work, Zod at every boundary, and a
shared package holding the EIP-712 struct definitions. Chain, compliance,
anchoring and identity are interfaces with a real and a mock implementation
selected by env var, so the test suite never depends on a public network being
up while the deployed instance always uses the real one. API and web run on
Render, the database on Supabase, the workflow on a Chainlink DON, the
contracts on Hedera testnet.

CHAINLINK CRE, AND THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN

The identity match runs in a Confidential Workflow on a TEE. The obvious design
was "encrypt the vendor record, decrypt inside the enclave, compare it." That
is impossible. The CRE SDK bans node:crypto outright, and the declared globals
are only TextEncoder/Decoder, Buffer, atob/btoa, URL and console. No
crypto.subtle, nothing. There is no primitive inside the enclave to decrypt
with.

So we inverted it. At onboarding we store HMAC(pan, pepper) and
HMAC(normalise(legalName), pepper). At match time the API hashes the sender's
typed values the same way, and the enclave compares digest against digest. No
crypto is needed inside because the hashing already happened outside. The
pepper never leaves our server and the enclave never sees an identity. It is
not that the enclave is trusted with PII, it is that there is no PII in it to
leak.

The cost is real and worth stating. Exact digests remove the near-miss band, so
a typo is now a flat mismatch rather than a 0.95 similarity score. We think
that is a net gain, because fuzzy name matching is precisely how a lookalike
payee slips through. Normalisation does the work instead: "MERIDIAN COMPONENTS
PRIVATE LIMITED" and "Meridian Components Pvt Ltd" reduce to the same digest.

The second CRE problem is that the HTTP trigger is fire and forget.
workflows.execute returns an execution id and nothing else, and there is no API
to read a workflow's return value, so a workflow cannot be called as a
synchronous "is this payee verified?" RPC. The workflow POSTs its verdict to a
callback endpoint and the caller awaits the database row. That suits the
confidential design rather than fighting it, because the verdict is exactly the
one value that is supposed to leave the enclave.

The callback has to be idempotent. In DON mode every observing node runs the
handler and every node POSTs the same verdict, so five callbacks arrive for one
logical answer. In TEE mode exactly one does. Both are correct, so later
callbacks are accepted and ignored.

One trap worth naming: a CRE execution reaching SUCCESS only means the handler
did not throw. A matcher that always answered MATCHED would look identical
across every case. Our end to end script therefore asserts the verdict for five
different inputs rather than the execution status. The enclave authenticates to
the vendor lookup with a JWT held in the Vault DON and released directly into
the attested enclave.

HEDERA

Three separate uses, each doing something the others cannot.

The tokenised bond is deployed with the Asset Tokenization Studio with
internalKycActivated set to true. That single flag is the integration: false and
the token enforces nothing, leaving grantKyc with nothing to gate. The issuing
account holds the KYC_MANAGER, INTERNAL_KYC_MANAGER and SSI_MANAGER roles and is
registered as an issuer, without which grantKyc reverts with AccountIsNotIssuer.
The demonstration that matters is the failure: a transfer to a wallet that never
went through grantKyc reverts on chain, not in our validation.

The cash leg is an HTS fungible token moving through an HTLC contract. HTS
tokens answer the ERC-20 interface at their long zero address, 0x followed by
the token number in hex padded to 40 characters, which is how viem can talk to
them at all. Accounts are created with maxAutoAssociations set to -1, because a
receiver with no free association slots rejects an incoming token transfer. The
balance card surfaces that field for exactly this reason.

Evidence anchoring uses the Consensus Service. Records are batched into a Merkle
tree and the root is submitted to a topic. Anchoring then reads itself back from
a mirror node and compares the published root against the recorded one. Mirror
nodes lag consensus by a few seconds, so the read back retries briefly, but a
root mismatch throws immediately and is never retried away: a disagreement
between our row and the public record is the one failure this whole mechanism
exists to surface.

WORLD ID

Selfie Check, with signals role qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>. This is not cosmetic. The nullifier uniqueness index is
(nullifier, action, signal), so a bare payment id means one human acting as both
sides of a payment collides with their own earlier proof. The asymmetry is
deliberate too: the sender is checked on every payment unconditionally, while
the payee is challenged only on risk, because the payee is the counterparty and
friction there costs you the payment.

HACKY AND NOTABLE

The EIP-712 structs live in one shared package imported by the signer, the
verifier and the tests. A second copy that merely reorders two fields produces
signatures that fail with no useful error, because the recovered address is
simply a different address.

Next.js rewrites default to afterFiles, which runs only when no page matched. We
had pages at /vendors and /payments, so the API proxy was silently shadowed:
calls returned 200 with Next's HTML, JSON.parse produced a string, and the first
visible symptom was an undefined id three steps later. beforeFiles fixes it.

The API's token minting endpoint is registered only when NODE_ENV is not
production, deliberately, because an approver token is what stands between a
payment and a human agreeing to it. That broke the entire deployed app, since
the web console minted its own tokens. The fix is a Next route handler signing
HS256 tokens server side for two roles only, agent and approver, never issuer or
bridge. The JWT is hand rolled with node:crypto rather than adding a library,
because the payload is two claims and a new dependency means a lockfile change
on a deployment that installs with a frozen lockfile.

grantKyc is idempotent. The chain outlives our database and the wallet key lives
in the browser's localStorage, so a reset database plus a reconnected wallet
asks the chain for a state it is already in. The contract answers with a bare
custom error revert that surfaces as an unhelpful 500. A grant is a state, not
an event.

Every foreign key is onDelete: Restrict, so evidence is never silently orphaned.
Even wiping the demo database has to be done in strict reverse dependency order.

DigiLocker returned a 403 whose body we were deliberately withholding from logs
to avoid leaking PII. The actual message was "Insufficient credits." We now
surface the message and transaction id only, never the data. Separately, a user
who grants Aadhaar consent but not PAN produced an opaque 400 much later, so
there is now a pre-flight scope check naming the document that is missing.
auto_summary: A monorepo app that verifies payees, gates token transfers with Hedera compliance, uses World ID checks, and settles approved payments via HTLC escrow.
